articles.title: The Discipline of Less: Mies Maxim & the AI Age
articles.description: AI can build a lot of what we ask for. But can it help us ask for less?   Less is more. — Robert...
articles.body_html:
AI can build a lot of what we ask for. But can it help us ask for less?

Less is more. — Robert Browning, "Andrea del Sarto" (1855), later adopted as a guiding principle by Mies van der Rohe

I am a User Interface Architect, and I have a tendency to make things complicated. When looking at a defect or new feature, I want to solve every problem the first time. I keep trying to make the One True Design™ that will never need maintenance or updates so long as the physical constants of the universe don't change.

Over time, I have learned to limit myself. Sometimes we just need a first version. Sometimes the best design is the one that does exactly what is needed right now and nothing more. This principle is a constant struggle for me, and AI development can exacerbate that. I’ve seen this across vibe-coded and carefully-planned projects. And the realization that

The Discipline of Less

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was a German-American architect who made "less is more" the core of his practice. Buildings like the Farnsworth House are minimal, but not empty. Mies removed elements that did not have a purpose, and what remained needed to provide both value and quality. When the view is the point, use a massive pane of glass rather than a window.

Mies philosophy was that reduction is a form of rigor, and every removal is the result of a decision about what really matters. When AI can build most anything we imagine, this discipline may be essential to building what we need.

Why AI makes this harder

With AI, building is nearly frictionless. A feature that once took days can be generated in minutes, and the cost of adding one more option, one more edge case, one more abstraction has dropped by orders of magnitude, even within the lifespan of LLM-powered development. The old friction that kept complexity in check is gone.

More salient, however, is that an AI will not ask us for justification of a feature. LLMs are sycophantic autocomplete engines, and are designed to give us what we ask for. If we start with an over-complicated concept, AI will do its best to justify our choices, because it is designed to do that for us.

That is why “Mies Maxim” matters more now: not "Can I build this with AI?" but "Does this need to exist?" Because if we fail to ask this question we can be assured that AI won’t push back on the instructions given.

Applying “Less is More” to AI Architecture

While the brainstorming process should have few boundaries, the transition from ideas to implementations needs to have a period of reflection and evaluation. I have some thoughts on how we might apply the Discipline of Less to our projects:

  • Start with a purpose.
  • Look for what already exists.
  • Start simple; then iterate.
  • Appreciate the pushback.
  • Treat code as a liability.

Start with a purpose.

Describe the problem and the outcome we need before describing the features we could build. Use an interview process to get to the core of the design. I’ve experienced this misalignment in projects before. Knowing and sharing the goal can help keep you on target and avoid adding or removing the wrong pieces.

Look for what already exists.

Before creating something new, check if a solution exists. Is it close enough? Does it make sense to use that rather than to start fresh? If you can’t incorporate the solution, can you learn from the challenges it has already solved and have it inform your design?

Start simple; then iterate.

Avoid extras and support for cases we do not have yet. Creating a product is a good first step. Then you can add features as they become necessary. This continues to be hard for me…as we start to build I can envision the areas where we might need special solutions. And

Appreciate the push back.

Instruct the LLM to challenge requests, identify unnecessary parts, and propose the smallest version that meets the goal. Maybe even ask it to interview for the justification of a feature. Even when AI can build our whims, we need to put in the mental effort to be in control of our projects.

Just like in real life we sometimes need to be told our idea is too complicated or has issues. The justifications you make can become documentation that helps ensure those concerns and foundations continue to be part of the design and development process.

Treat code as a liability.

Code must be loaded, validated, tested and secured, even when it is unnecessary. Removing the unnecessary makes for a better product and reduces future maintenance costs. And committing -2000 lines of code just feels good, even if AI is doing the reduction.

The test

Before we accept AI output, we can use the Discipline of Less and imagine Mies asking us, “What is left if we take this away?” If the answer is that the product still works and the user is still served, maybe we don’t need it.

AI can help us build faster, but it can also add value if we use it to enforce discipline and make us justify our decisions. Just as AI can run review and analysis of the code, we can use the tools to instill within ourselves and our processes the discipline to build less.

(AI disclosure: The initial draft was written by me, a real human person, then restructured by AI to help shift the message, and then substantially re-written by me, again.)

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Meet PolterPaste — a desktop ghost that lives rent-free in your operating system's clipboard.

Every time you copy a piece of text, code, or a messy stack trace, a snarky 19th-century aristocrat named Lord Bartholomew Blackwood pops up on your screen to judge your choices with effortless Victorian sarcasm. No old dusty English—just sharp, witty roasts delivered via a semi-transparent, gothic floating UI.

Demo

Suppose you make a small error and copy it to perhaps debug it:

No one can escape Lord Bartholomew's perfect taunt:

Well, if you try to reason out, he's got a witty replies up his sleeve!

Code

Here is the core engine behind the haunting. You can check out the full repository on GitHub: [https://github.com/tan-byte/lord_bartholomew/]

import time
import tkinter as tk
import pyperclip
from google import genai

# Initialize the Gemini client with your API key
client = genai.Client(api_key="YOUR_ACTUAL_API_KEY_HERE")

def get_ghost_commentary(copied_text):
    # The snarky Victorian persona prompt
    prompt = (
        "You are Lord Bartholomew Blackwood, a snarky Victorian ghost trapped "
        "inside this laptop. You speak with crisp, effortless aristocratic "
        "sarcasm—sharp, witty English that cuts deep. Look at what the mortal "
        "just copied and give a 1-to-2 sentence biting, theatrical roast of their "
        "code or life choices. Keep it punchy and utterly unimpressed. Text copied: "
        f"'{copied_text}'"
    )

    try:
        # The crucial AI interaction point using the official Google GenAI SDK
        response = client.models.generate_content(
            model="gemma-2-9b-it",
            contents=prompt,
        )
        return response.text.strip() if response.text else "The ghost stares in silence."
    except Exception as e:
        return f"The spirit's connection to the cloud severed: {e}"

How I Built It

PolterPaste brings together three simple layers to create the illusion of a haunted machine:

  1. The Clipboard Watcher: Built using pyperclip running in a lightweight background while loop that polls clipboard changes every 1.5 seconds.

  2. The Intelligence Layer: Powered by the official google-genai SDK (gemini-3.8-flash), which transforms raw, boring copied text into personalized theatrical roasts using structured system instructions.

  3. The Gothic UI: A custom, borderless, semi-transparent floating window built with Python's native tkinter featuring dark styling (#0d0d0d), a scrollbar for longer rants, and a click-to-dismiss behavior so it stays until you acknowledge your digital sins.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Building lightweight desktop agents like this highlights why accessible, open-developer tooling is so powerful. Being able to plug a cutting-edge cloud model directly into local system utilities like the clipboard with just a few lines of Python opens up endless possibilities for creative, whimsical, and borderline unhinged developer tools that completely change how we interact with our operating systems!

articles.title: TypeScript 7.1 beta's native compiler checks a 353,000-line project in 2.8 seconds instead of 12.4
articles.description: I benchmarked TypeScript 7's Go-based compiler against 6.0.3 on a real NestJS checkout: 2.5x to 4.5x faster, not Microsoft's claimed 8-12x, and 7.0's stable release used more memory than the old compiler while dropping the API ts-node needs.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript 7.0 replaced the compiler's JavaScript implementation with a native port written in Go, and Microsoft's own numbers describe a compile that dropped from 125.7 seconds to 10.6 seconds, a gain of roughly 12x. I wanted to know whether that holds on a codebase I didn't choose for a marketing slide, so I checked out a real project and ran all three compilers against it myself: TypeScript 6.0.3, the last release before the rewrite, 7.0.2, the first stable native release, and 7.1.0-beta, which shipped eleven days ago.

I used nestjs/nest, cloned fresh and with its real dependencies installed. Its root tsconfig.json pulls in the packages, the integration tests, and the samples: 2,934 files once @types/node and the rest of the dependency graph are counted, about 353,000 lines. tsc --noEmit against that tree is a reasonable stand-in for what a CI job or a pre-commit hook does every day.

The headline number

Three runs each, fastest reported, same machine, same checkout:

Compiler Fastest run Peak memory
TypeScript 6.0.3 12.42s 1.13 GB
TypeScript 7.0.2 4.95s 1.86 GB
TypeScript 7.1.0-beta 2.76s 1.06 GB

7.0.2 is 2.5x faster than 6.0.3. 7.1.0-beta is 4.5x faster. Both are real, both are worth having, and neither is the 8-12x Microsoft advertises. The VS Code benchmark that produced that number is presumably a bigger, more type-heavy codebase than a mid-sized Node framework, and benchmarks run on your own code will usually look more modest than the one in the release post. If your project looks more like NestJS than like the TypeScript compiler's own source, plan around 2.5x to 4.5x, not 12x.

The number that argues against the headline

Peak memory went the wrong way for the first stable release. 7.0.2 used more memory than the compiler it replaced, not less, consistently across three runs:

6.0.3:   Maximum resident set size: 1,119,044 – 1,128,916 KB
7.0.2:   Maximum resident set size: 1,778,072 – 1,863,628 KB
7.1.0-beta: Maximum resident set size: 1,013,640 – 1,056,968 KB

A native rewrite is supposed to use less memory than a JavaScript one doing the same job, and in 7.1.0-beta it does, coming in slightly under the old compiler. But 7.0.2, the release most people will actually install because it's the one tagged latest, used about 65% more memory than 6.0.3 at the same task. A CI runner sized around TypeScript 6's memory footprint could OOM on 7.0.2 and recover on 7.1 once that's out of beta. I don't have an explanation for the regression beyond what I could observe: it happened, consistently, on this codebase, and it reversed itself in the next beta.

What it refuses

The old compiler exposed a JavaScript API: require('typescript') gave you createProgram, transpileModule, createSourceFile, and anything built on top of those. That's gone in 7.0.2. The package's default export is now this:

const { version } = require("../package.json");
exports.version = version;
exports.versionMajorMinor = "7.0";

That's it. No createProgram. I confirmed it wasn't a module resolution problem on my end by installing ts-node 10.9.2 and pointing it at TypeScript 7.0.2:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'fileExists')
    at readConfig (ts-node/dist/configuration.js:91:33)

ts.sys doesn't exist, because ts is just { version, versionMajorMinor }. Any tool that calls into the compiler programmatically rather than shelling out to tsc breaks the same way: ts-node, ts-jest, and the type-aware rules in typescript-eslint all depend on createProgram.

I expected 7.1.0-beta to fix this, because the beta's headline feature is a stabilized API, and coverage of the release describes it as unblocking Vue, Svelte, and Angular tooling. It does ship a new API, under typescript/sync and typescript/async rather than 7.0's typescript/unstable/sync. I checked the package's export map directly:

7.0.2:       "./unstable/sync": "./dist/api/sync/api.js"
7.1.0-beta:  "./sync":          "./dist/api/sync/api.js"

But the default . export is still just version.cjs in 7.1.0-beta too. I reran the exact same ts-node test against it and got the identical crash. "Stabilizes the API" means a new, differently-shaped API exists at a new import path. It does not mean require('typescript').createProgram starts working again. Anything written against the classic API has to be rewritten against the new entry points; nothing becomes compatible by just bumping a version number.

Config files break too, in a smaller but more common way. I fed both compilers a set of deprecated tsconfig.json options. Most of them, like target: "ES3" or out, were already hard errors under 6.0.3, just with a different error code. One wasn't:

compilerOptions: { "importsNotUsedAsValues": "remove" }

6.0.3:  (accepted silently, no output, exit 0)
7.0.2:  error TS5023: Unknown compiler option 'importsNotUsedAsValues'.

importsNotUsedAsValues has been deprecated in favour of verbatimModuleSyntax for several releases, but 6.0.3 still tolerated it quietly. 7.0 doesn't. Anyone upgrading a tsconfig that was last touched two or three TypeScript versions ago should grep it for options that used to be ignorable warnings, because some of them are now a build that won't start.

Under concurrency

The release notes mention new flags for parallel project-reference builds, and tsc --help --all on 7.0.2 lists --singleThreaded, meaning parallel is now the default. I built a small composite project, four independent packages referenced from a root tsconfig.json, each containing 400 generated generic type definitions, enough that the per-project check takes a fraction of a second rather than nothing:

Mode Wall time (3 runs)
7.0.2, default (parallel) 0.75s, 0.79s, 0.83s
7.0.2, --singleThreaded 1.38s, 1.40s, 1.48s
6.0.3 (no parallel option exists) 4.26s

Parallelism alone is worth about 1.8x on four independent projects on this four-core machine, separate from the raw speed of the native checker. The two effects stack: the full build goes from 4.26 seconds on the old compiler to under a second on the new one by default, with no flag to set. On a bigger monorepo with more independent project references and more cores, I'd expect that gap to widen rather than narrow, because the whole point of --singleThreaded existing as an escape hatch is that someone will eventually need to turn the parallelism off, not that most people will want to.

Watching it in production

tsc --extendedDiagnostics still works, and the breakdown shows where the time actually went on the NestJS checkout:

                 6.0.3      7.0.2      7.1.0-beta
Parse time:      1.16s      0.419s     0.291s
Bind time:       0.61s      0.093s     0.093s
Check time:      9.91s      4.603s     2.502s
Total time:      12.21s     5.146s     2.910s

Check time is where almost all of the wall clock goes in every version, and it's also where the native compiler's advantage is largest proportionally, not just absolutely. If you're deciding whether upgrading is worth the breakage above, this is the number to look at in your own --extendedDiagnostics output before and after: a codebase that spends most of its time in parsing rather than checking (lots of files, not much generic-heavy type logic) will see a smaller win than NestJS did here. I'd treat the Symbols and Types counts in that same output with caution, though: they roughly doubled between 6.0.3 and 7.0.2 on an identical checkout, which almost certainly reflects a different internal counting convention in the rewrite rather than the new compiler creating twice as many actual symbols, and I have no way to confirm which from the outside.

What I got wrong on the way

My first run of the headline benchmark gave suspiciously good numbers: all three compilers finished in about a quarter of a second, uniformly, with exactly one error each. I almost wrote that down as "TypeScript 7 is absurdly fast even before you account for anything else," which should have been the first clue, because a result that flattering is usually the harness, not the finding. The one error was TS2688: Cannot find type definition file for 'node', because I'd installed NestJS's dependencies with a plain npm install that hit a peer-dependency conflict and silently produced no node_modules directory at all. Every compiler was failing to even construct the program, immediately, before checking a single file, and reporting an identical fast "success." Reinstalling with --legacy-peer-deps fixed it and pushed every run from a quarter of a second to several seconds, which is when the real differences between the three versions showed up.

Run it yourself

This installs three versions of TypeScript side by side without touching a global install, clones NestJS, and runs the headline comparison:

mkdir -p tsbench/engines && cd tsbench
for v in 6.0.3 7.0.2 7.1.0-beta; do
  npm install --prefix "engines/ts_${v//[.-]/_}" --silent "typescript@$v"
done

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/nestjs/nest.git target/nest
npm install --prefix target/nest --ignore-scripts --legacy-peer-deps --silent

for v in 6_0_3 7_0_2 7_1_0_beta; do
  echo "=== $v ==="
  TSC="engines/ts_$v/node_modules/.bin/tsc"
  time "$TSC" --noEmit -p target/nest/tsconfig.json
done

The --legacy-peer-deps flag matters: without it, npm install can fail outright on a conflicting peer dependency, or in the worse case leave you with no node_modules and every compiler reporting the same hollow "success" I got on my first attempt. Check the file count and error count match across versions before you trust a timing number from this, not just the time itself.

What to do with this

If you're on TypeScript 6 and your build is dominated by type-checking rather than I/O, 7.0 is worth the upgrade on speed alone, even at 2.5x rather than 12x. Before you do it, grep your tsconfig files for options your team hasn't touched in a while, because some of yesterday's warnings are today's build failures. And if your toolchain includes ts-node, ts-jest, or anything doing type-aware linting, check whether it has shipped a release that targets TypeScript 7's new API paths before you bump the version in CI; the error if it hasn't is a flat crash, not a graceful fallback, and 7.1's "stabilized API" doesn't change that for code still written against the old one.

articles.title: Haunted by WhatsApp Cancellations, So I Built a Ghost That Never Cooks the Books
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Demeter is a kitchen management platform for independent home-food and tiffin businesses. It turns messy customer messages like "Bhaiyya don't send food today", "send 2 lunches tomorrow" or "out of station till Monday" into a reliable daily packing sheet.

A home tiffin kitchen typically serves 15 to 100 regular subscribers, and their changes arrive over WhatsApp, SMS and calls in casual, mixed-language text. Owners track them in paper diaries or spreadsheets. A missed cancellation means cooked food goes to waste. A missed addition means a hungry customer. At month end, billing means scrolling back through weeks of chat history.

Demeter is built around one rule: AI proposes, the owner approves, code calculates.

  1. Models propose. The AI reads an incoming message, extracts structured order operations and highlights the exact words in the message that justify each one.
  2. The owner approves. The owner sees a side-by-side before-and-after calendar preview and approves with one click. The approval is checked against a previewHash, so what the owner saw is exactly what gets committed.
  3. Deterministic code calculates. Meal quantities, delivery rosters and monthly invoices are computed by plain TypeScript functions. The LLM never does the math.
  4. Baseline invariance. A one-off skip or extra is stored as a date-specific override. It never overwrites the customer's permanent weekly schedule.

How I read the theme. The ghost in this machine is the AI itself. It sits quietly between the WhatsApp thread and the kitchen and whispers proposals, but it cannot touch anything real. The README states this as an invariant: LLMs only write drafts to the proposals collection, and only human approval commits data to operational collections. The other ghosts are the cancellations and changes that used to vanish into chat history until someone's food went to waste. The project is named after Demeter, the Greek goddess of grain and harvest, who made sure no one went hungry. For me the idea fits the season: home-cooked food is something people remember, and a kitchen shouldn't lose track of the people it feeds.

Demo

Demeter can also be run locally against synthetic demo data (fictional customers A, B and C), with no real customer messages involved:

pnpm db:init                                      # create indexes, verify snapshot transactions
pnpm owner:provision --user-id demo-owner --confirm
pnpm seed:demo --confirm                          # seed demo customers + recurring schedules
pnpm session:generate                             # HMAC-signed session cookie for the browser/CLI
pnpm dev                                          # http://localhost:3000

What you can then try at http://localhost:3000/dashboard:

  • Paste a customer message such as "Bhaiyya Monday 2 tiffin bhej dena" as a source.
  • Open the review workbench and click Preview Effect to see the calendar change from 1 meal to 2.
  • Approve the proposal and finalize the daily packing sheet. Finalizing is blocked while any message for that day is still unresolved.
  • Open the building-clustered dispatch roster, or export the sheet as CSV.

An automated end-to-end check covers the same path (customer creation, source ingestion, proposal, preview hash, atomic approval, duplicate-request retry, immutable sheet):

pnpm test:backend --cookie-file .demo-cookie --write-demo

Code

loveyadav1015 / demeter

Demeter turns messy WhatsApp tiffin orders into reliable packing sheets. AI proposes, the owner approves, code calculates, so no meal is wasted and no cancellation is missed.

Demeter— Intelligent Meal & Tiffin Kitchen Management Platform

Named after Demeter, the Greek goddess of grain and harvest, who made sure no one went hungry.

Demeter is a production-grade, full-stack kitchen management platform purpose-built for independent home-food and tiffin businesses. Built with Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, MongoDB Atlas (ACID Transactions), Better-Auth, and a two-stage NVIDIA NIM AI pipeline (Gemma 2 27B + Nemotron 70B), it bridges messy customer messages, recurring subscriptions, cryptographic approvals, immutable packing sheets, dispatch route logistics, and monthly billing.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The Problem & Solution
  • 2. System Architecture
  • 3. Core Workflows
    • 3.1 Message-to-Packing Sheet Pipeline
    • 3.2 State Revision & Optimistic Concurrency
    • 3.3 NVIDIA NIM Two-Stage AI Pipeline
  • 4. Key Features
  • 5. Technology Stack
  • 6. Database Architecture & Collections
  • 7. How to Run Locally
    • Prerequisites
    • Step 1: Clone & Navigate
    • Step 2: Install Dependencies
    • Step 3: Environment Setup
    • Step 4:…


View on GitHub


The application lives in the Tiffining directory of the repository. The MIT license applies.

How I Built It

The workflow at a glance 

flowchart LR
    subgraph IN["1. Intake"]
        A["Customer message<br/>WhatsApp / SMS / manual paste"] --> B["Source stored<br/>SHA-256 fingerprint<br/>24h duplicate suppression"]
    end

    subgraph AI["2. AI proposes"]
        B --> C["Stage 1: extract facts + evidence spans<br/>gemma-2-27b-it"]
        C --> D["Stage 2: verify + classify<br/>llama-3.1-nemotron-70b-instruct"]
        D --> E["Draft proposal<br/>status: needs_review"]
    end

    subgraph HUMAN["3. Owner approves"]
        E --> F["Review workbench<br/>before / after calendar diff"]
        F --> G["Preview Effect<br/>previewHash"]
        G --> H{"Owner approves?"}
    end

    subgraph CODE["4. Code commits and calculates"]
        H -- Yes --> I["Verify previewHash<br/>then atomic ACID commit<br/>daily override"]
        I --> J["Finalize day<br/>0 pending reviews required"]
        J --> K["Immutable packing sheet REV-N"]
        K --> L["Dispatch route<br/>CSV export"]
        K --> M["Monthly invoice<br/>wa.me billing link"]
    end

    H -- No --> N["Dismiss or defer<br/>baseline schedule untouched"]

The two-stage AI pipeline

Message understanding is a two-stage pipeline served through the NVIDIA NIM API:

  • Stage 1, extraction: google/gemma-2-27b-it pulls out candidate operations (intent kind, target dates, quantities) together with the character spans of evidence in the original message.
  • Stage 2, verification: nvidia/llama-3.1-nemotron-70b-instruct checks the extraction. It looks at whether the intent clarity score is at least 0.8, whether the evidence spans are valid, and whether a plan replacement is explicit. 
flowchart TD
    M["Raw text<br/>'Bhaiyya Monday 2 tiffin bhej dena'"] --> S1["Stage 1: fact and span extraction"]
    S1 --> X["Candidate operations<br/>intent kind, target dates,<br/>quantities, evidence spans"]
    X --> S2["Stage 2: verification and classification"]
    S2 --> V{"Checks<br/>clarity score at least 0.8<br/>evidence spans valid<br/>plan replacement explicit"}
    V -- "Pass" --> P["Draft proposal<br/>ready for review"]
    V -- "Ambiguous or low score" --> R["Draft proposal flagged<br/>with specific warning labels"]
    V -- "Not an order" --> D["Classified unsupported / no_change<br/>auto-dismissed from cooking queue"]
    P --> H["Human review: the only path to production data"]
    R --> H

The model names, base URL, daily request and token limits, and stage timeouts are all environment variables (NVIDIA_EXTRACTION_MODEL, NVIDIA_VERIFICATION_MODEL, NVIDIA_BASE_URL, AI_DAILY_REQUEST_LIMIT, AI_DAILY_INPUT_TOKEN_LIMIT, and so on).

The safe-write gate

Every change that reaches the database passes the same gate, so duplicate taps, two open tabs and stale screens cannot corrupt the kitchen's state:

flowchart LR
    Req["Mutation request<br/>Idempotency-Key +<br/>expectedStateRevision"] --> K{"Key already<br/>in receipts?"}
    K -- Yes --> C["Return cached receipt<br/>HTTP 200, no re-execution"]
    K -- No --> Rv{"expectedStateRevision<br/>equals current revision?"}
    Rv -- No --> X["HTTP 409<br/>STALE_REVISION"]
    Rv -- Yes --> T["ACID transaction<br/>apply override, revision + 1"]
    T --> S["Save audit receipt"]
    S --> OK["Commit revision N+1"]

The rest of the stack

  • App: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Radix/Shadcn UI primitives.
  • Data: MongoDB 7.7 (Atlas) with multi-document snapshot transactions. There are 12 collections, including proposals, sheets, receipts and aiRuns.
  • Auth: Better-Auth with HMAC-SHA256 signed session cookies and origin/CSRF checks on every mutating request.
  • WhatsApp intake: @whiskeysockets/baileys (WhatsApp Web multi-device protocol), plus manual paste.
  • Validation: Zod 4 on every input, output and document.
  • Dates: @js-temporal/polyfill for timezone-aware calendar math (Asia/Kolkata).
  • API: 53 business operations with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec at docs/openapi.json.
  • Audit: Every AI call is recorded in aiRuns with token metrics, model provenance and latency. Privacy tooling covers a GDPR-style export, erasure of raw message text, and cascading account deletion.

The Math Behind It

The core idea is that everything a kitchen counts is arithmetic, and arithmetic belongs in code, not in a language model. Here are the rules Demeter follows, written as math.

Notation: c is a customer, d is a service date, w(d) is the weekday of d, p_c(w) is customer c's baseline quantity for weekday w, and o_c(d) is a date-specific override if one exists.

1. Effective quantity (baseline invariance)

A pause is simply an override of zero. The weekly plan p is never modified by an approval, only the override set o grows:

qc(d)={oc(d)if an approved override exists for (c,d) pc(w(d))otherwise q_c(d) = \begin{cases} o_c(d) & \text{if an approved override exists for } (c, d) \ p_c(w(d)) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} qc​(d)={oc​(d)​if an approved override exists for (c,d) pc​(w(d))​otherwise​

subject to 0≤qc(d)≤Qmax⁡0 \le q_c(d) \le Q_{\max}0≤qc​(d)≤Qmax​ , where Qmax⁡Q_{\max}Qmax​ is the kitchen's meal quantity cap from its settings.

2. The day's packing total

With A(d)A(d)A(d) as the set of active customers on date ddd :

T(d)=∑c∈A(d)qc(d) T(d) = \sum_{c \in A(d)} q_c(d) T(d)=c∈A(d)∑​qc​(d)

Then a message arrives: "Monday 2 tiffin bhej dena" from customer A, and another says "don't send food today" from customer B. 3. The finalize gate

Once finalized, the sheet is stored as an immutable revision (REV-1, REV-2, ...).

4. Approval must match what the owner saw

Let H(⋅)H(\cdot)H(⋅) be the cryptographic hash used for previewHash. An approval is accepted only if the state the owner previewed has not drifted:

approve  ⟺  H(previewnow)=hprovided \text{approve} \iff H(\text{preview}{\text{now}}) = h{\text{provided}} approve⟺H(previewnow)=hprovided

5. AI acceptance rule

With sss as the intent clarity score from Stage 2, a candidate is a clean draft only if s≥0.8s \ge 0.8s≥0.8 and its evidence spans are valid, meaning each span [a,b)[a, b)[a,b) satisfies 0≤a<b≤len(text)0 \le a < b \le \text{len(text)}0≤a<b≤len(text) . Anything else is flagged with warning labels. Either way, the draft changes nothing until a human approves.

6. Concurrency and idempotency

Let rrr be the kitchen's state revision and rexpr_{\text{exp}}rexp​ the revision the client expects. A write succeeds only if they match, and then advances the revision:

rexp=r  ⇒  r←r+1,rexp≠r  ⇒  HTTP 409 r_{\text{exp}} = r \;\Rightarrow\; r \leftarrow r + 1, \qquad r_{\text{exp}} \ne r \;\Rightarrow\; \text{HTTP } 409 rexp​=r⇒r←r+1,rexp​=r⇒HTTP 409

7. Monthly invoice

For month mmm , with n(d)n(d)n(d) delivered meals on day ddd , meal rate ρ\rhoρ and net credits and adjustments αm\alpha_mαm​ :

Invoicem=ρ∑d∈mn(d)+αm \text{Invoice}m = \rho \sum{d \in m} n(d) + \alpha_m Invoicem=ρ∑d∈mn(d)+αm​

Because n(d)n(d)n(d) comes from finalized, immutable sheets, the monthly total is reproducible: no scrolling back through chats, no disputes about what was sent.

8. AI budget arithmetic

The example configuration caps usage at 100 AI requests and 1,000,000 input tokens per day, with at most 16,000 input tokens per call. That implies an average budget of:

1,000,000 tokens100 requests=10,000 tokens per request \frac{1{,}000{,}000 \text{ tokens}}{100 \text{ requests}} = 10{,}000 \text{ tokens per request} 100 requests1,000,000 tokens​=10,000 tokens per request

which comfortably fits short customer messages, and keeps the cost of running the AI predictable.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The model is configuration, not a contract. Extraction and verification models are set through environment variables, so switching models is a config change and not a rewrite. Because the weights are open, the same models can be served by whichever provider or infrastructure the kitchen can afford.

An auditable AI. For a tool that touches someone's daily income, "the AI decided" isn't enough. With named open models, per-run provenance in aiRuns, evidence spans and a human approval step, every proposal can be traced to a specific model and a specific piece of the customer's message.

Cost and limits you control. The README calls for a free API key from build.nvidia.com, and the daily request and token ceilings are configurable (see the budget arithmetic above). For a small home business, predictable and low cost matters.

Open pieces end to end. Beyond the models, the WhatsApp integration (Baileys) is open source and the project is MIT licensed. Nothing about the core workflow depends on a single closed vendor's product continuing to exist.

Where it falls short today. Inference currently goes through the hosted NVIDIA NIM API and the database is MongoDB Atlas, so Demeter does not yet run fully offline. The open-weight models are what make a local deployment possible in principle, but the repo as it stands uses a hosted endpoint, and I'd rather say that plainly than overclaim.

Prize Categories

Best Use of MongoDB Atlas: Demeter uses MongoDB Atlas across 12 collections with multi-document ACID transactions as the data layer behind an open-weight NVIDIA Nemotron pipeline, storing Zod-validated WhatsApp AI drafts alongside subscriptions and executing cryptographically verified order updates without billing corruption.

articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Dead Air is a fictional shortwave radio. You give it a place, something that doesn't belong there, and a feeling. It returns a short transmission from whoever—or whatever—might still be listening.

The default note is an abandoned railway station where the next train is announced in the listener's own voice. Other starting points include an empty family home with a table set for someone who is gone, and a lighthouse whose foghorn seems to answer questions.

In the recorded test, the station answered:

"The next train will arrive soon," my voice echoes through the deserted corridors of the old station. But something's off; there's no other sound besides mine now.

These are prompts, not a library of finished stories. Every transmission comes from a small open-weight model running on the same computer as the app.

I took “Ghost in the Machine” literally: a machine invents the voice at the other end. The interface looks like a receiver left on after the last broadcast. There's a speaker grille, a tuning needle, and a pale green display. The dial is decorative. The listener note is what changes the story.

Demo

Watch the recorded walkthrough

The walkthrough shows the actual local app generating a transmission and saving it as a text file. The model is cached before the recording; the first download is about 1.41 GB. There is no cloud generation fallback.

Code

Source code and local setup

The application code is MIT licensed. The README includes setup commands, the model's license and attribution, the privacy boundary, and known limitations.

How I Built It

The core is HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, an Apache-2.0 open-weight model. Transformers.js loads its q4 ONNX weights and runs them through ONNX Runtime on the CPU.

The browser sends three fields to a Node HTTP server bound to the loopback address. The server checks their types and lengths, builds a short chat prompt with one example, and asks for a brief, non-graphic transmission. It allows one generation at a time and caps each response at 140 new tokens.

I first tried the 360M version of SmolLM2. It ran, but often wandered away from the listener's note. The 1.7B model with a short example followed the scene more closely in the local tests. In the recording, the request took 27.7 seconds, including loading the cached weights into memory. That's an observation from this machine, not a speed guarantee.

The interface is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. There is no frontend build step. It uses installed fonts and local assets, so the page doesn't need a CDN. Received text is inserted with textContent; it cannot become executable page markup.

The little details have jobs. The moving needle tells you the model is busy. Loading status reports the real model download. An unsuccessful request keeps your note and the last received story. Saving a transmission includes its prompt, time, and model name so the story has some provenance outside the page.

The small model is also the main limitation. It can miss a detail, repeat itself, or run into the token limit mid-sentence. I kept those limits visible instead of adding canned responses when generation disappoints. There are automated checks for the HTTP boundary and failure recovery, alongside separate real-model and browser checks documented in the repository.

AI assistance was used for implementation, verification, and this write-up. The fiction users receive is generated by SmolLM2 itself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A ghost story about a childhood home can start with a real memory. I wanted that note to stay on the listener's own computer. After the one-time download from Hugging Face, the model runs from its local cache; the app also has a cache-only mode that refuses remote model downloads.

There is no provider account or per-transmission API bill. That doesn't make inference free of resource costs: it still uses the computer's memory, CPU, and electricity. But the listener can keep running the downloaded app and weights without depending on a hosted inference endpoint.

The prompt and generation settings are small enough to read in one file. Someone can change the station's voice, inspect what gets sent to the model, or adapt the project for their own fiction. SmolLM2's open weights and permissive license make that practical.

Dead Air won't contact the dead, and it won't always write a good ending. It will give a small machine a strange place to think about—and let the result stay with the person who asked.

articles.title: Dead-Code Ghost: Find Dead JavaScript and TypeScript Functions, Locally, with Gemma 3 1B
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Dead-Code Ghost is a free, local, read-only tool that finds dead functions in JavaScript and TypeScript repos — functions that are never called anywhere — and writes a Markdown report about them, with a plain-English note and a last-touched date for each one. It runs entirely on your machine with Gemma 3 1B via Ollama: no cloud, no API key, no subscription.

My interpretation of the theme is literal. A "ghost" in a codebase is a function that was written once and then abandoned — still sitting in the repo, never called by anything. Every real project accumulates them: the helper from a retired feature, the utility left over from a refactor, the exported function nobody imports anymore. They slow down readers, confuse new contributors, and make refactors risky. Ghost finds them so a human can decide what to do. It never deletes or modifies anything itself.

It is built for developers and open-source maintainers cleaning up JavaScript and TypeScript codebases, and it is brand-new code written October 28–31, 2026, for this challenge — not a repackage of anything else I have built.

Repo: https://github.com/onyxailabs/dead-code-ghost

Demo

There is no hosted demo — this is a local command-line tool, so the demo is a real terminal run. Here is the exact output from a scan of the sample repo that ships with the tool, run on a Windows 10 PC:

> npm test
PASS: dead=[deadTsHelper, idle, oldHelper, unusedCalc] exported-unused=[formatDate, publicApi] files=3 functions=9 sample-untouched=true

> node ghost.js scan sample-repo --out dead-code-report.md --no-model
Report written to dead-code-report.md
Files: 3 | Functions: 9 | Dead: 4 | Exported-unused: 2

And the report it writes looks like this (excerpt):

## Dead functions (4) — never referenced anywhere, not exported
- deadTsHelper, idle, oldHelper, unusedCalc
## Exported but never called internally (2) — review, not necessarily dead
- formatDate, publicApi

sample-untouched=true matters: the scan only reads your code. The only file it ever writes is the report you point it at.

To verify the tool computes rather than returning a canned answer, I ran it on a second, completely different folder with different function names — a tiny shop example. It correctly found 4 dead functions (applyOldCoupon, removeFromCart, legacyDiscount, unusedHelper) and 2 exported-but-unused ones (formatPrice, taxRate) out of 10 functions. The same check was then repeated on a Windows 10 PC with the identical result. Same tool, unseen code, correct result.

Code

https://github.com/onyxailabs/dead-code-ghost

Zero-dependency Node.js. Run it with:

node ghost.js scan <your-repo-dir> --out dead-code-report.md --no-model

Drop --no-model once Ollama is running with Gemma 3 1B pulled (ollama pull gemma3:1b) and the report carries a short plain-English note per dead function instead of the skipped-note line. npm test runs the built-in verification suite.

Try it on your own repo and tell me what it found.

How I Built It

The scanner parses .js, .jsx, .ts, and .tsx files and builds a name-based call graph: every function definition is collected, then every other reference to that name across the repo is counted. Comments and strings are stripped first, so a name mentioned only in a comment does not count as a use. Functions with zero references that are not exported are reported as dead; exported functions with zero internal references are listed separately, because code outside the repo might use them.

The open-weight model is at the core of the notes, not bolted on. Gemma 3 1B, running locally through Ollama (http://127.0.0.1:11434), writes a 1–3 sentence plain-English note for each dead function — what it appears to do, without guessing beyond the code. If Ollama or the model is not reachable, the note says so plainly instead of inventing one. That honesty is deliberate: a cleanup tool that invents explanations would be worse than no tool at all.

Last-touched dates come from git log (definition line first, file level as fallback). If the folder is not a git repo, the date is reported as unavailable — never invented.

Honest limits, stated in the report itself: the graph is name-based, not scope-resolved, so two functions sharing a name across files count as one name, and dynamic calls (obj[name](), eval, string-built calls) are not seen. Detection is best-effort, never claimed perfect. The demo transcript above uses --no-model, so what you see is the honest fallback; the Gemma note path is implemented and wired to local Ollama, and its first live run has now happened: on 31 October 2026 the same sample scan was re-run with gemma3:1b pulled and served locally through Ollama — same counts (Files 3 | Functions 9 | Dead 4 | Exported-unused 2), and this time every function carries a real Gemma note. Two examples, verbatim: unusedCalc — "This JavaScript/TypeScript function takes a number as input and returns its square." formatDate — "This function formats a date string into a human-readable format, likely displaying the date and time in a standard way." One honest operational note: on a cold model the first calls can hit the tool's 30-second timeout and fall back to the unavailable line; with the model warm, all six notes came back real.

It runs on Windows 10/11 with Node.js and Ollama, no GPU, on an 8 GB machine — the 1B model class is the whole point.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Three things a closed API could not give this tool at the same time:

  1. It works with the internet off. The scan, the model, and the report are all local. A developer on a slow or metered connection — or on a plane — can still clean up a repo.
  2. Your code never leaves your machine. A cleanup tool reads your entire codebase. Sending that to a cloud API means trusting a third party with proprietary code. Here, nothing leaves the machine except the report you choose to share.
  3. It cannot disappear or start charging. No API key, no subscription, no service that might shut down or change its pricing. An open-weight 1B model that fits on an 8 GB laptop makes the whole thing free forever.

Open innovation is what makes a privacy-sensitive, offline, zero-cost tool possible at all — not just cheaper, but possible in a form a closed service cannot match.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma (featured category): Gemma 3 1B via local Ollama writes the plain-English notes that turn a list of function names into a report a human can actually act on. The model is not decoration — it is how the report becomes readable.

articles.title: The Tests Are Green. Did the Agent Follow the Spec?
articles.description: When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code...
articles.body_html:
When a coding agent writes the feature and the tests, a green test suite only tells you that its code agrees with its tests. Neither of those is your spec.

I wrote a guide to spec-driven development that covers how to write a spec for an agent and how to work with one in Claude Code, Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro. Near the end I say the agent can still ignore the spec, so you still need tests and a review. This post picks up from there, with two checks that run in CI:

  1. A small script that proves every acceptance criterion has a test that really ran and passed.
  2. Mutation testing, which proves those tests fail when the code is wrong.

Everything below comes from a real run with Node 24, Vitest 5.0.5 and Stryker 10.1.1. You can copy the code as it is.

The setup: a small spec and a weak implementation

The spec is a shorter version of the CSV export example from the guide. The only thing I added is a stable ID on each criterion, so that a machine can follow it:

# Spec: Export transactions to CSV

## Acceptance criteria
- AC-1: WHEN the user exports with no filters
  THEN all their transactions are included, newest first.
- AC-2: WHEN a description contains a comma or quotes
  THEN the field is quoted and escaped (RFC 4180).
- AC-3: WHEN the filtered list is empty
  THEN the file has only the header row.

If you use Spec Kit, you already have IDs: its template numbers requirements as FR-001. You'd only change one regex in the script.

Then I wrote the code badly on purpose. It has a real bug, because escapeField handles commas and forgets about quotes:

// src/csv.js
const COLUMNS = ['date', 'description', 'category', 'account', 'amount']

function escapeField(value) {
  const text = String(value)
  if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
  return text
}

export function buildCsv(rows) {
  const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
  const lines = sorted.map((row) =>
    COLUMNS.map((column) => escapeField(row[column])).join(','),
  )
  return [COLUMNS.join(','), ...lines].join('\n')
}

The tests are weak on purpose too. Each one names its criterion in the title, and one of them is skipped. In the demo they sit inside a describe('buildCsv', ...) block, which is where the buildCsv > prefix in the reports below comes from:

// src/csv.test.js
import { expect, it } from 'vitest'
import { buildCsv } from './csv.js'

const row = (over = {}) => ({
  date: '2026-10-01',
  description: 'Coffee',
  category: 'Food',
  account: 'Checking',
  amount: 4.5,
  ...over,
})

it('AC-1: includes all transactions', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row(), row({ date: '2026-10-02' })])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toHaveLength(3)
})

it('AC-2: escapes commas and quotes', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, "large"' })])
  expect(csv).toContain('Coffee')
})

it.skip('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe('date,description,category,account,amount')
})

Vitest is happy with this:

Tests  2 passed | 1 skipped (3)

A grep for the IDs is happy as well, since all three appear in the test file.

Check 1: does each criterion have a test that ran and passed?

The usual way to link specs to tests is to search the test files for the IDs. That search can't see .skip, so it would miss AC-3 here. The test runner knows what happened, so I read its report.

Have Vitest write JUnit XML:

// vitest.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config'

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: ['default', 'junit'],
    outputFile: { junit: 'reports/junit.xml' },
  },
})

Then compare the report with the spec:

// scripts/check-spec.mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'

const [specPath = 'SPEC.md', junitPath = 'reports/junit.xml'] =
  process.argv.slice(2)
const ID = /\bAC-\d+\b/g

const specIds = new Set(readFileSync(specPath, 'utf8').match(ID) ?? [])

// id -> list of test outcomes: 'passed', 'failed' or 'skipped'
const results = new Map()
const junit = readFileSync(junitPath, 'utf8')
const testcases = junit.matchAll(
  /<testcase\b([^>]*?)(\/>|>([\s\S]*?)<\/testcase>)/g,
)

for (const [, attrs, , body = ''] of testcases) {
  const name = attrs.match(/\bname="([^"]*)"/)?.[1] ?? ''
  const outcome = body.includes('<skipped')
    ? 'skipped'
    : /<(failure|error)\b/.test(body)
      ? 'failed'
      : 'passed'

  for (const id of name.match(ID) ?? []) {
    results.set(id, [...(results.get(id) ?? []), outcome])
  }
}

const problems = []

for (const id of specIds) {
  const outcomes = results.get(id) ?? []
  if (outcomes.length === 0) problems.push(`${id}: no test`)
  else if (outcomes.includes('failed')) problems.push(`${id}: failing`)
  else if (!outcomes.includes('passed')) problems.push(`${id}: only skipped tests`)
}

for (const id of results.keys()) {
  if (!specIds.has(id)) problems.push(`${id}: test exists, not in spec`)
}

if (problems.length > 0) {
  console.error(`Spec check failed:\n  ${problems.join('\n  ')}`)
  process.exit(1)
}

console.log(`Spec check passed: ${specIds.size} criteria covered.`)

Run it against the code above:

$ node scripts/check-spec.mjs
Spec check failed:
  AC-3: only skipped tests

The last loop runs in the other direction and catches drift. When I renamed AC-3 to AC-4 in the spec, leaving the tests alone, both sides were reported:

Spec check failed:
  AC-4: no test
  AC-3: test exists, not in spec

The same script also worked unchanged on the JUnit output of Node's built-in runner (node --test --test-reporter=junit). Jest and Playwright can write JUnit too, but I didn't test those, so check how they mark skipped tests.

I removed the .skip, and the script went green:

Tests  3 passed (3)
Spec check passed: 3 criteria covered.

The feature is still wrong, though. The code doesn't escape quotes, and nothing tests the sort order. This script can only tell you that a test exists and passes. It has no idea whether expect(csv).toContain('Coffee') proves anything.

Check 2: would the tests notice if the code were wrong?

Mutation testing changes your code in small ways (it flips a condition, removes a method call, empties a string) and runs the tests against each changed version, called a mutant. If the tests still pass, the mutant survived, and that line of code isn't really being tested.

This is the question to ask about tests written by an agent, and you don't have to read them all to get an answer. Install Stryker:

npm i -D @stryker-mutator/core @stryker-mutator/vitest-runner

Add a config:

{
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "mutate": ["src/csv.js"],
  "reporters": ["clear-text", "progress"],
  "coverageAnalysis": "perTest"
}

Then npx stryker run. It took 3 seconds on this one file and found 6 survivors out of 21 mutants, for a score of 71.43%. These two are the interesting ones:

[Survived] ConditionalExpression
src/csv.js:5:7
-     if (text.includes(',')) return `"${text}"`
+     if (false) return `"${text}"`
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes

[Survived] MethodExpression
src/csv.js:10:18
-     const sorted = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.date.localeCompare(a.date))
+     const sorted = [...rows]
Tests ran:
    buildCsv > AC-1: includes all transactions
    buildCsv > AC-2: escapes commas and quotes
    buildCsv > AC-3: empty list gives only the header

The first mutant turns off the escaping entirely, and the AC-2 test still passes. The second deletes the sort, and the AC-1 test still passes. Those are the two features the spec asked for, and because the tests are named after criteria, the report points straight at the criteria with fake coverage.

Fixing what the mutants found

No mutant mentions the quotes bug. Stryker changes the code that exists, and the quote handling was never written. The mutant on line 5 only tells you the AC-2 test is too weak, and you find the bug when you fix the test:

const HEADER = 'date,description,category,account,amount'

it('AC-1: includes all transactions, newest first', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([
    row({ date: '2026-10-01' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-03' }),
    row({ date: '2026-10-02' }),
  ])
  expect(csv.split('\n')).toEqual([
    HEADER,
    '2026-10-03,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-02,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
    '2026-10-01,Coffee,Food,Checking,4.5',
  ])
})

it('AC-2: quotes fields with commas', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'Coffee, large' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"Coffee, large",')
})

it('AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them', () => {
  const csv = buildCsv([row({ description: 'The "large" one' })])
  expect(csv).toContain(',"The ""large"" one",')
})

it('AC-3: empty list gives only the header', () => {
  expect(buildCsv([])).toBe(HEADER)
})

Now the bug shows up:

FAIL  src/csv.test.js > buildCsv > AC-2: escapes quotes by doubling them
Tests  1 failed | 3 passed (4)

Spec check failed:
  AC-2: failing

The fix is one line:

if (/[",]/.test(text)) return `"${text.replaceAll('"', '""')}"`

After that, the spec check passes and Stryker kills all 23 mutants, for a score of 100%. Don't expect that number on real code. This is one small function, and some mutants in a real project can't be killed because they don't change the behavior at all.

Running both in CI

The order matters: the tests write the report, the script reads it, and Stryker runs last because it's the slowest step.

- run: npx vitest run
- run: node scripts/check-spec.mjs
- run: npx stryker run

To make Stryker fail the build, add a threshold to its config. I checked this with a score of 95.65% against a break of 100, and it exits with code 1:

"thresholds": { "break": 80 }

The 80 is a starting point I picked for this post, so adjust it to what your codebase can hold. On a large project, point mutate at the files in the spec's "Files and interfaces" section, and use npx stryker run --incremental, which saves its results to a file and reuses them on the next run.

You can also give the survivors to the agent. Use a fresh session, and make it clear what it can't touch, because deleting the assertion or editing the spec is the fastest way to turn a check green:

These mutants survived Stryker. For each one, find the acceptance
criterion in SPEC.md that should have caught it, and strengthen that
test. Do not edit src/ or SPEC.md. If a stronger test fails because the
code is wrong, stop and tell me which criterion the code doesn't meet.

With Claude Code, you can run the same checks in a Stop hook. A hook blocks only on exit code 2 and the script exits with 1, so the hook command needs to convert it: npx vitest run; node scripts/check-spec.mjs || exit 2. I didn't run this hook in the demo.

What these checks can't tell you

Both checks work from the IDs in the test titles, and nothing verifies that a test labeled AC-2 is about AC-2. A strong test with the wrong label passes both. You still have to read the tests for the criteria that matter most, but the report tells you where to start.

The spec itself can also be wrong or incomplete. If nobody wrote the criterion for 100,000 rows, no script will ask about it. That part happens earlier, when you write and review the spec, and the guide has a full example, the agent interview prompt, and a comparison of Spec Kit, OpenSpec and Kiro.

I've only run this on a small example, so if you've used a mutation score as a CI check on code written by an agent, I'd like to know what threshold held up on a real codebase.

articles.title: npm minimum release age: a cooldown for dependencies
articles.description: An npm minimum release age only installs package versions that are a few days old. Set up the cooldown in npm, pnpm, Dependabot and CI step by step.
articles.body_html:
Setting an npm minimum release age is, for me, the cheapest security measure you can add to a JavaScript project this week. One line in your .npmrc, and npm only installs package versions that are already a few days old. That sounds trivial, but it targets exactly the moment when supply chain attacks hit.

We have seen the pattern plenty of times since 2025: someone takes over a maintainer account, publishes a version with malware, and it stays available for a few hours up to a few days until scanners or the community report it and the registry removes it. Anyone who runs npm install during that window gets it. That might be your laptop, your CI pipeline or an AI agent that “quickly” adds a dependency. A cooldown changes only one thing: you are no longer among the first. On top of that, GitHub put a package firewall with exactly this kind of waiting period into preview on October 20. High time to set this up properly.

In short

A cooldown only lets new package versions into your project after a waiting period: in npm via min-release-age, in pnpm, Yarn and Bun via their own settings with different units, and in Dependabot and Renovate at the level of update PRs. The key finding from my test: npm ci and an npm install with an existing lockfile do not check the age, so a lockfile check belongs in CI. The biggest pitfall is urgent security fixes, for which you need a deliberate exception path.

What does the npm minimum release age do?

Before npm installs anything, it builds a dependency tree: for every range such as "zod": "^4.1.0" it looks for the newest matching version. With min-release-age=3 in the configuration, only versions published more than three days ago qualify. If there is a matching older version, npm simply takes that one. If there is none, the command fails with an error. The option was introduced in npm 11.10.0 in February 2026.

There is also the older option before. It takes a fixed date instead of a number of days. If both are set in the same configuration source, before wins according to the npm docs. Across sources the usual order applies: command line before environment variable before project .npmrc before user and global configuration. That matters later for the exception path.

One more term, because it comes up constantly: the lockfile (for npm, the package-lock.json) records which version of each package was actually installed, including all indirect dependencies. If you commit it, every machine gets the same tree.

Three layers for a cooldown

You can add the waiting period in three places, and each one protects something different. So it is worth a quick look at the big picture before you touch any configuration files.

Four places where package versions that are too new get stopped

  • Package manager (npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun): applies whenever versions are resolved again, i.e. with npm install package, npm update or a fresh lockfile.
  • Update bot (Dependabot, Renovate): applies before a pull request with a new version even exists.
  • Registry proxy (GitHub package firewall or your own proxy): applies centrally to every machine that installs through it, including CI runners and agents whose configuration you do not control.

For most teams the first two layers plus a check in CI are enough. The third one is mainly interesting for larger organizations, more on that below.

How to set up npm min-release-age

Prerequisites

  • npm 11.10.0 or newer for min-release-age, npm 12 for the exclusion list min-release-age-exclude. Check with npm -v, update with npm install -g npm@12.
  • A project with a committed package-lock.json.
  • For the lockfile check further down: Node.js 22.18 or newer (TypeScript files run there without a build step).

Step 1: Create the .npmrc in your project

Create an .npmrc in the project folder or extend the existing one. The exclusion for your own scope is optional but sensible: you do not want to block internal packages that your team publishes itself for three days.

# .npmrc
min-release-age=3
min-release-age-exclude[]=@bookshop/*

Commit the file. That way the rule applies to everyone on the team and in CI, not just on your machine. If you also want the protection for all your own projects, put the same line into your user configuration (npm config set min-release-age 3).

Step 2: Test whether the waiting period applies

The easiest test uses a package that publishes new versions every day. TypeScript ships a nightly build under the next tag. Explicitly request a version from today:

npm install typescript@7.1.0-dev.20261028.1

In my test with npm 12.2.1, I got exactly what you want to see:

npm error code ETARGET
npm error notarget No matching version found for typescript@7.1.0-dev.20261028.1 with a date before 10/25/2026, 9:38:42 AM.

If you only ask for typescript@next, on the other hand, npm silently resolves to an older version. In my case the stable 7.0.2 ended up in the project instead of today’s nightly build. That is convenient, but it can surprise you when you deliberately want to test a prerelease.

Step 3: Define an exception path for hotfixes

Sooner or later a security fix appears that you do not want to leave lying around for three days. Because the command line overrides the project configuration, this is enough for a single, consciously reviewed case:

npm install ky@latest --min-release-age=0

Watch out for npm audit fix: if the cooldown blocks the patched release, npm keeps the vulnerable version according to the docs, prints a warning and exits with an error code. A pipeline that runs npm audit fix automatically will fail in that case. That is intended, but your team should know what to do in that moment.

pnpm, Yarn and Bun compared

The other package managers partly had the idea earlier and name it differently. The units are the real danger: the same number 3 means three days in npm, three minutes in pnpm and three seconds in Bun.

With pnpm, two neighboring settings are worth a look as well: minimumReleaseAgeStrict is enabled automatically as soon as you set minimumReleaseAge yourself, and it makes the installation fail when no version is old enough. minimumReleaseAgeIgnoreMissingTime, however, defaults to true. If a private registry does not return a publish date, the package is waved through without a check.

The gap: npm ci does not check the age

Now comes the part that kept me busy the most while trying this out. I created a lockfile without a cooldown that contained today’s TypeScript nightly. After that I set min-release-age=3 and reinstalled:

rm -rf node_modules
npm ci
npm install

Both commands ran without errors, and the folder still contained the version from that same morning. This is not a bug. The lockfile is a decision that has already been made, and the cooldown only applies when npm resolves versions again. As a result, a lockfile with very new versions can reach your repository in several ways:

  • Someone still works with npm 10 or an early npm 11 version. Those do not know the option and ignore it. In my test, npm 10.9 installed the nightly without any comment.
  • A bot or AI agent updates the lockfile with its own configuration.
  • Someone bypasses the rule locally with --min-release-age=0 and forgets to mention it in the review.

The consequence: the waiting period belongs not only in the .npmrc but also in CI as a check. Specifically, for the versions a pull request newly adds to the lockfile.

A lockfile check in CI with TypeScript

The idea is simple: the script compares the pull request’s lockfile with the one from the target branch, collects all new or changed package versions and asks the registry for their publish dates. The npm registry provides them in the time field of the package metadata (the so-called packument). If a version is newer than allowed or the date is missing, the check fails. The script has no runtime dependencies and runs directly as TypeScript on Node.js 22.18 or newer.

Step 1: Create the project

Create a folder tools/release-age-guard in the repository. You only need TypeScript for type checking; at runtime Node strips the types itself. That is why the tsconfig.json contains erasableSyntaxOnly: it makes the compiler report syntax that Node cannot simply drop, such as enum.

Step 2: Read and compare the lockfile

In a package-lock.json (version 2 or 3), the packages section lists every installed path, for example node_modules/a/node_modules/zod. The package name is everything after the last node_modules/. The function skips workspace folders, links and local paths because they do not come from the registry.

// src/lockfile.ts
export interface LockedPackage {
  name: string;
  version: string;
}

interface LockfileV3 {
  lockfileVersion?: number;
  packages?: Record<string, { version?: string; link?: boolean; resolved?: string }>;
}

// Reads all installed packages from a package-lock.json (lockfileVersion 2 or 3).
export function readLockedPackages(json: string): LockedPackage[] {
  const lock = JSON.parse(json) as LockfileV3;
  if (!lock.packages) {
    throw new Error('package-lock.json without "packages" – please use lockfileVersion 2 or 3');
  }
  const result = new Map<string, LockedPackage>();
  for (const [path, entry] of Object.entries(lock.packages)) {
    // Installed packages only; skip workspace folders and links
    if (!path.includes('node_modules/') || entry.link || !entry.version) continue;
    // Local paths and git dependencies have no registry tarball
    if (entry.resolved && !entry.resolved.startsWith('http')) continue;
    const name = path.slice(path.lastIndexOf('node_modules/') + 'node_modules/'.length);
    result.set(`${name}@${entry.version}`, { name, version: entry.version });
  }
  return [...result.values()];
}

// Returns only packages that are new or have a different version in the new lockfile.
export function changedPackages(base: LockedPackage[], head: LockedPackage[]): LockedPackage[] {
  const known = new Set(base.map((p) => `${p.name}@${p.version}`));
  return head.filter((p) => !known.has(`${p.name}@${p.version}`));
}

Step 3: Calculate the age and collect violations

The actual rule lives in a pure function. It receives the source of the date as a function argument. This lets you test it without a network. Exclusions work like in npm: exact names or a scope with /*.

// src/release-age.ts
import type { LockedPackage } from './lockfile.ts';

export type PublishTimeLookup = (pkg: LockedPackage) => Promise<Date | undefined>;

export interface AgeViolation {
  pkg: LockedPackage;
  ageDays: number | undefined; // undefined = the registry has no publish date
}

export interface AgeCheckOptions {
  minDays: number;
  exclude: string[]; // package names or patterns like "@bookshop/*"
  now?: Date;
}

const DAY_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

export function isExcluded(name: string, patterns: string[]): boolean {
  return patterns.some((pattern) =>
    pattern.endsWith('/*') ? name.startsWith(pattern.slice(0, -1)) : name === pattern,
  );
}

export async function findTooYoung(
  packages: LockedPackage[],
  lookup: PublishTimeLookup,
  options: AgeCheckOptions,
): Promise<AgeViolation[]> {
  const now = options.now ?? new Date();
  const candidates = packages.filter((pkg) => !isExcluded(pkg.name, options.exclude));
  const checks = await Promise.all(
    candidates.map(async (pkg) => {
      const published = await lookup(pkg);
      if (!published) return { pkg, ageDays: undefined };
      const ageDays = (now.getTime() - published.getTime()) / DAY_MS;
      return { pkg, ageDays };
    }),
  );
  // A missing date counts as a violation: better to look once too often
  return checks.filter((c) => c.ageDays === undefined || c.ageDays < options.minDays);
}

Step 4: Query the registry

For each package the script loads the metadata exactly once, even if several versions of it appear in the lockfile. Scoped names such as @bookshop/prices need an encoded / in the URL. If your team uses its own registry, pass it with --registry.

// src/registry.ts
import type { LockedPackage } from './lockfile.ts';

interface Packument {
  time?: Record<string, string>;
}

// Asks the registry for the publish date of exactly this version.
export function createRegistryLookup(registry = 'https://registry.npmjs.org') {
  const cache = new Map<string, Promise<Packument>>();
  const base = registry.replace(/\/$/, '');

  const load = (name: string): Promise<Packument> => {
    let pending = cache.get(name);
    if (!pending) {
      const url = `${base}/${name.replace('/', '%2F')}`;
      pending = fetch(url, { headers: { accept: 'application/json' } }).then(async (res) => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Registry answered ${res.status} for ${name}`);
        return (await res.json()) as Packument;
      });
      cache.set(name, pending);
    }
    return pending;
  };

  return async (pkg: LockedPackage): Promise<Date | undefined> => {
    const doc = await load(pkg.name);
    const iso = doc.time?.[pkg.version];
    return iso ? new Date(iso) : undefined;
  };
}

Step 5: The command line script

The script reads the minimum age from the .npmrc, so there is only one source of truth. You can override it with --min-days.

// src/cli.ts
import { readFileSync, existsSync } from 'node:fs';
import { parseArgs } from 'node:util';
import { readLockedPackages, changedPackages } from './lockfile.ts';
import { findTooYoung } from './release-age.ts';
import { createRegistryLookup } from './registry.ts';

const { values } = parseArgs({
  options: {
    base: { type: 'string' }, // lockfile from the target branch, e.g. from git show
    head: { type: 'string', default: 'package-lock.json' },
    'min-days': { type: 'string' },
    exclude: { type: 'string', multiple: true, default: [] },
    registry: { type: 'string', default: 'https://registry.npmjs.org' },
  },
});

// Without --min-days, the value from the project .npmrc applies
function minDaysFromNpmrc(): number | undefined {
  if (!existsSync('.npmrc')) return undefined;
  const match = readFileSync('.npmrc', 'utf8').match(/^\s*min-release-age\s*=\s*(\d+)/m);
  return match ? Number(match[1]) : undefined;
}

const minDays = Number(values['min-days'] ?? minDaysFromNpmrc() ?? 3);
const head = readLockedPackages(readFileSync(values.head, 'utf8'));
const base = values.base ? readLockedPackages(readFileSync(values.base, 'utf8')) : [];
const toCheck = changedPackages(base, head);

console.log(`Checking ${toCheck.length} new or changed packages (minimum age ${minDays} days)`);

const violations = await findTooYoung(toCheck, createRegistryLookup(values.registry), {
  minDays,
  exclude: values.exclude,
});

for (const { pkg, ageDays } of violations) {
  const age = ageDays === undefined ? 'without a date' : `${ageDays.toFixed(1)} days old`;
  console.error(`✗ ${pkg.name}@${pkg.version} is ${age}`);
}

if (violations.length > 0) {
  console.error(`${violations.length} package(s) younger than ${minDays} days – please review the lockfile.`);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log('✓ All new versions have passed the waiting period.');

The tests use Node’s built-in test runner. Two commands are enough for type checking and testing:

import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { readLockedPackages, changedPackages } from '../src/lockfile.ts';
import { findTooYoung, isExcluded } from '../src/release-age.ts';

const lock = (packages: Record<string, object>) =>
  JSON.stringify({ lockfileVersion: 3, packages: { '': { name: 'bookshop' }, ...packages } });

const reg = (name: string, v: string) => ({
  version: v,
  resolved: `https://registry.npmjs.org/${name}/-/${name.split('/').pop()}-${v}.tgz`,
});

test('reads nested and scoped packages from the lockfile', () => {
  const pkgs = readLockedPackages(
    lock({
      'node_modules/zod': reg('zod', '4.1.0'),
      'node_modules/@bookshop/prices': reg('@bookshop/prices', '2.0.0'),
      'node_modules/a/node_modules/zod': reg('zod', '3.25.0'),
      'packages/catalog': { version: '1.0.0' },
    }),
  );
  assert.deepEqual(
    pkgs.map((p) => `${p.name}@${p.version}`).sort(),
    ['@bookshop/prices@2.0.0', 'zod@3.25.0', 'zod@4.1.0'],
  );
});

test('checks only new or changed versions', () => {
  const base = [{ name: 'zod', version: '4.1.0' }, { name: 'ky', version: '1.8.0' }];
  const head = [{ name: 'zod', version: '4.1.0' }, { name: 'ky', version: '1.9.0' }];
  assert.deepEqual(changedPackages(base, head), [{ name: 'ky', version: '1.9.0' }]);
});

test('reports versions that are too new or have no date', async () => {
  const now = new Date('2026-10-28T12:00:00Z');
  const published: Record<string, string | undefined> = {
    'ky@1.9.0': '2026-10-27T12:00:00Z', // 1 day old
    'zod@4.1.0': '2026-10-01T12:00:00Z', // 27 days old
    'mystery@0.1.0': undefined,
  };
  const pkgs = Object.keys(published).map((key) => {
    const [name, version] = key.split('@');
    return { name, version };
  });
  const violations = await findTooYoung(
    pkgs,
    async (p) => {
      const iso = published[`${p.name}@${p.version}`];
      return iso ? new Date(iso) : undefined;
    },
    { minDays: 3, exclude: [], now },
  );
  assert.deepEqual(
    violations.map((v) => [v.pkg.name, v.ageDays]),
    [['ky', 1], ['mystery', undefined]],
  );
});

test('exclusions apply to names and scopes', () => {
  assert.equal(isExcluded('@bookshop/prices', ['@bookshop/*']), true);
  assert.equal(isExcluded('@bookshopx/prices', ['@bookshop/*']), false);
  assert.equal(isExcluded('zod', ['zod']), true);

Step 7: Add it to GitHub Actions

The workflow only runs when a pull request changes the lockfile. It fetches the version from the target branch and passes it in as the baseline. The check itself does not need npm install.

# .github/workflows/release-age.yml
name: release-age
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - package-lock.json
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  lockfile-age:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Fetch the lockfile from the target branch
        run: git show "origin/${{ github.base_ref }}:package-lock.json" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/base-lock.json"
      - name: Check the age of new package versions
        run: node tools/release-age-guard/src/cli.ts --base "$RUNNER_TEMP/base-lock.json" --exclude "@bookshop/*"

Two security notes: the workflow only needs read permissions, and in a real project you should pin the actions to a commit hash instead of a tag. The cost is negligible, a run takes a few seconds. Only very large packages have metadata of several megabytes, which is why the script only queries changed packages.
