Dependabot cooldown and Renovate minimumReleaseAge

The update bots are the second layer. They make sure that no pull request with a brand-new version is created in the first place, and they are the reason the lockfile check rarely fires in everyday work.

Dependabot

According to the current GitHub docs, Dependabot already applies a three-day waiting period to version updates by default. With the cooldown block you can fine-tune it, separately for major, minor and patch updates. Security updates are explicitly excluded and arrive immediately.

# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 3
      semver-major-days: 14
      semver-minor-days: 7
      semver-patch-days: 3
      exclude:
        - "@bookshop/*"

Renovate

Renovate calls the option minimumReleaseAge and expects a duration as text. As long as a version is too new, Renovate does not create a branch at all with the default setting internalChecksFilter: "strict". When generating the npm lockfile, Renovate also passes --before itself, so indirect dependencies are not too fresh either. Here, too, security updates bypass the waiting period.

{
  "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  "extends": ["config:recommended"],
  "minimumReleaseAge": "3 days",
  "packageRules": [
    { "matchUpdateTypes": ["major"], "minimumReleaseAge": "14 days" },
    { "matchPackageNames": ["@bookshop/**"], "minimumReleaseAge": null }
  ]
}

Since Renovate 42, a missing timestamp counts as “not old enough yet”. For npm this is not an issue, but with some container registries Renovate holds back digest updates indefinitely as a result. My rule of thumb for both bots: the waiting period in the bot is at least as long as the one in the .npmrc. Otherwise you get pull requests that could not even be reproduced locally with a fresh install.

GitHub package firewall for larger organizations

On October 20, 2026, GitHub released the package firewall as a public preview. It sits between your machines and the npm registry and checks both metadata requests and downloads against policies that administrators define for the whole enterprise. These include a configurable waiting period, checks against the GitHub Advisory Database for malware and vulnerabilities, and checks such as a downgrade in attestations. If the firewall blocks a package by mistake, developers can request an exception.

The limitations are clear: so far it only supports npm and is only available to GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers. It is free during the preview and is supposed to be billed by usage afterwards. I mainly see its appeal for agents and CI runners whose configuration you do not control in every repository. For a single team it does not replace the three configuration files from this article; it complements them.

How long should the cooldown be?

My recommendation to start with: three days in the package manager, and in the bot three days for patches, seven for minor and 14 for major updates. The three days are not arbitrary. The npm registry allows authors to unpublish a package within 72 hours of publishing it. If you wait three days, you no longer install a version that might still disappear at short notice. Majors get more time because they mean work anyway and an extra week rarely matters.

I often hear two objections. The first: “If everyone waits, who will find the malicious version?” In the well-known cases from 2025, it was mostly the automated scanners of security companies that raised the alarm first, since they analyze every new version right away. The early installers were victims rather than discoverers. Still, the objection is not entirely unfounded, so I would not go up to several weeks. The second objection: “Then security fixes arrive too late.” For the bots that is not true, because security updates bypass the waiting period. Locally you need the deliberate exception path from step 3.

Where I clearly disagree: a cooldown is no substitute for other measures. It does not help against packages that have been malicious for a long time, nor against install scripts of packages you trust anyway. A committed lockfile, npm ci in the pipeline, install scripts only for approved packages and trusted publishing for your own packages remain mandatory. The cooldown only takes the most dangerous moment off your hands: the first day of a new version. How quickly such a moment can escalate is something I described in the article on the Node.js vulnerability Node2Shell, even though that one was a flaw in Node itself.

Common mistakes with an npm cooldown

  • Mixing up units: minimumReleaseAge: 3 in pnpm means three minutes. Add the unit as a comment.
  • Old npm version on the team: npm before 11.10 ignores the option without an error. Set the minimum version in engines and check it in CI.
  • Exclusion too broad: an entry in the exclusion list only applies to the name, not to its dependencies. For hotfixes, prefer a targeted --min-release-age=0 on the single command.
  • Missing timestamps: private registries or proxies do not always return a time field. pnpm waves such packages through by default; the lockfile check from this article reports them.
  • Only the .npmrc, no check: without a CI check, new versions slip through existing lockfiles, see above.

FAQ

What is npm min-release-age?

An npm configuration option that defines how many days old a package version must be before npm installs it. Newer versions are skipped during resolution.

Which npm version introduced min-release-age?

The option arrived with npm 11.10.0 in February 2026. The exclusion list min-release-age-exclude has been available since npm 12.

Does min-release-age apply to npm ci?

No. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says. In my test, npm install with an existing lockfile also ran without an age check. That is why checking new lockfile entries in CI is worth it.

Does a cooldown delay security updates?

Not with Dependabot and Renovate; both exclude security updates. Locally and in the pipeline you need a deliberate exception path, for example --min-release-age=0 for exactly one command.

articles.title: Eight products, one URL: what breaks when a storefront has no router
articles.description: A static storefront serving eight products from a single /product page. Canonical collapse, missing structured data, social cards that never render, and the price that lived in four places. Real numbers, no framework.
articles.body_html:
I build a browser-side customizer for printed sneakers. You upload artwork, it gets sliced across the shoe panels, and you preview it on the actual shoe before ordering: bukefootwear.com. The geometry is in the first post, the magnification math in the second, the render pipeline in the third, the deploy budget in the fourth.

This one is about the storefront shell around it. Our release is a folder of static files on Cloudflare Pages. There is no router, no server, no /product/[slug] route. Eight shoe styles are served by one HTML file:

https://bukefootwear.com/product?product=KJ1
https://bukefootwear.com/product?product=MT1
...

That works fine for humans and it is a trap for everything else. Four things broke, and none of them threw an error.

1. Canonical collapse: eight pages that all claim to be the same page

The first version had no canonical at all. Then I added one — statically, into the <head> of product.html:

<link rel="canonical" href="https://bukefootwear.com/product">

Eight product URLs, one canonical target. To a crawler that says "these eight pages are duplicates of one page, index that one instead." Every individual style gets dropped. The page that ranks is a page with no product on it until JavaScript runs.

The fix is to make the canonical a function of the query string, and to accept that it is now JavaScript's job:

const code = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('product');
const canonical = document.createElement('link');
canonical.rel = 'canonical';
canonical.href = 'https://bukefootwear.com/product?product=' + encodeURIComponent(code);
document.head.append(canonical);

Two rules I now follow because of this:

  • Never ship a static canonical on a query-param page. A wrong canonical is worse than a missing one, and it is invisible in the browser.
  • The static HTML must never contradict what the JS writes. If a <link rel="canonical"> is already in the document, append gives you two canonicals and Google picks the first. The static one wins, and it is the wrong one.

The same shape of bug hit our designer page: it had <html lang="zh-CN"> and a Chinese <title>, and designer.js overwrote the title at runtime. Editing the HTML changed nothing for real visitors because the JS ran a millisecond later. Whatever the crawler reads statically and whatever the visitor sees have to be the same claim.

2. Zero structured data, on the pages that sell

Eight commercial pages, and the count of JSON-LD blocks across all of them was:

$ grep -c "application/ld+json" product.html
0

Not "malformed", not "warned in Search Console" — simply absent. Meanwhile the blog pages had it. The money pages were the only ones without a machine-readable name, price, or availability.

The reason was structural, not laziness: JSON-LD is per-product data, and a single static file cannot hold eight products' prices honestly. So it has to be generated where the product is known:

const ld = {
  '@context': 'https://schema.org',
  '@type': 'Product',
  name: `BUKE ${product.name} ${code}`,
  sku: code,
  brand: { '@type': 'Brand', name: 'BUKE STUDIO' },
  material: String(product.material || '').replace(/\s*[\r\n]+\s*/g, ', ').trim(),
};
if (images.length) ld.image = images.slice(0, 6);
if (fixedPrice && Number.isFinite(Number(fixedPrice.price))) {
  ld.offers = {
    '@type': 'Offer',
    price: Number(fixedPrice.price),
    priceCurrency: 'USD',
    url: 'https://bukefootwear.com/product?product=' + encodeURIComponent(code),
    availability: fixedPrice.purchasable
      ? 'https://schema.org/InStock'
      : 'https://schema.org/PreOrder',
    itemCondition: 'https://schema.org/NewCondition',
  };
}
const s = document.createElement('script');
s.type = 'application/ld+json';
s.textContent = JSON.stringify(ld);
document.head.append(s);

Two details that matter more than the schema itself:

The offers block is conditional. If the price is missing, emitting "price": undefined gives you {"@type":"Offer"} with no price — an invalid Offer that is worse than no Offer. Wrap the whole object, not the field.

material came from a text field with newlines in it. It arrived as "Upper: microfiber\nSole: rubber". Valid JSON, valid string, and a value no consumer wants to display. Normalise at the boundary, not at the renderer.

Verification has to be done in a real browser, because the block does not exist in curl output:

Product  sku=KJ1    price=98  USD  InStock  imgs=6
Product  sku=MT1    price=68  USD  InStock  imgs=6
Product  sku=DF1    price=88  USD  InStock  imgs=6

That is the same lesson as the canonical: if JavaScript writes it, only a JS-executing check counts. I have wasted more time on curl | grep returning empty while the browser was correct than on any other class of bug in this project.

3. Social cards never render, because crawlers do not run your JS

This one is specific and it bit us during a campaign. We were pushing a design challenge on Threads, X and Instagram. When someone shares a link, the platform fetches the URL, reads og:title, og:description, og:image from the raw HTML — and does not execute JavaScript.

Result: the links we were paying attention to, shared all day, rendered as bare text. No image. The tags we had were set by JS, therefore invisible to every scraper:

$ curl -s https://bukefootwear.com/challenge | grep -c 'og:image'
0

Three of our most-promoted pages (/product, /designer, /challenge) had zero or partial Open Graph tags. The homepage had them. The campaign pages did not.

The fix is unglamorous: static tags in the HTML, per page, with a real 1200px image, plus the Twitter variants because X does not read Open Graph:

<meta property="og:image" content="https://bukefootwear.com/assets/studio-v4/XB1-pair-1200.webp">
<meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
<meta property="og:image:height" content="1200">
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://bukefootwear.com/assets/studio-v4/XB1-pair-1200.webp">

And here is the honest trade-off: on a query-param storefront the static og:image is one image for all eight products. Scrapers cannot see the per-product image the JS picks. You either accept a generic card, or you generate eight real HTML files at build time.

I accepted the generic card for now. It is a small loss and an enormous improvement over nothing. The general rule: anything that must be readable by a machine that does not run JS (crawlers, social scrapers, link previews, RSS, some ad platforms) cannot be produced by client-side logic. Audit those separately; they are not part of your "the page works" test.

4. The price lived in four places

This is the one that would eventually have cost real money.

Prices for the eight styles were written into the product page markup, into a cart script, into a checkout calculation, and into one more place I found by grepping. They agreed, because I had been careful, which is exactly why the bug had not surfaced yet.

The data does not look risky:

// one module, the only place a price is allowed to be typed
window.BukePricing.products = {
  KJ1: { price: 98, purchasable: true },
  MT1: { price: 68, purchasable: true },
  ...
};

But a made-to-order shop has a twist: price and freight are different rules that both change. A pair costs $98. Shipping is charged once for the first pair and 40% for each additional one in the same order — so the number a customer sees depends on order composition, not on the product. Two formulas, two owners, and if either one is duplicated you get a cart that disagrees with the product page and nobody notices until a customer does.

What made this safe was not discipline. It was making the number impossible to type twice:

  • The product page renders price from the module.
  • The cart reads the same module.
  • The JSON-LD reads the same module.
  • Freight lives in exactly one function, and its constants are named, so "we changed the EU rate" is a one-line diff.

I now test pricing the same way I test pixels: change one value in the source of truth, reload three pages, and confirm all three moved. If one of them does not, I found a duplicate.

What a router would and would not have fixed

The reflexive answer is "use a framework with real routes." Eight static HTML files generated from one template would genuinely fix three of the four problems: real canonicals, real per-product Open Graph, no JS-dependent metadata. That is a build step, not a rewrite, and it is the correct destination.

It would not fix the fourth. A router does not create a single source of truth for price; it just moves the duplication. The rendering layer is the easy part — it is the data ownership that decides whether a storefront can be trusted with money.

Until then, the checklist I actually use before shipping a page that sells something:

  1. curl the URL and confirm canonical, description, title and Open Graph are all present in the raw HTML.
  2. Render it in a browser and confirm the JS-written versions match what curl returned, or that you accept the difference knowingly.
  3. Grep for the number. If the price appears in more than one file, that is the bug, whether or not it is wrong today.
  4. Count JSON-LD blocks. Zero on a commercial page is a decision you did not make on purpose.

The product pages these lessons came from are here, if you want to see the result: KJ1 low-top, MT1 slipper, and the designer that does the slicing.
